advisories.overview: Septoria tritici blotch (Zymoseptoria tritici) produces irregular, rectangular tan-to-brown lesions speckled with distinct tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) on wheat leaves.
symptoms: Scout lower leaves early in the spring for yellowish flecks expanding into tan rectangular blotches.
Use a 10x hand lens to confirm the presence of tiny black pimple-like pycnidia within lesions.
Track rain events during stem elongation that splash spores upward to upper leaves.

Avoid excessive nitrogen that produces thick, slow-drying crop canopies.
Ensure adequate field drainage.
prevention: Plant septoria-resistant or tolerant wheat cultivars adapted to your region.
Practice at least a 1-year rotation to non-host crops (canola, pulses, corn).
Avoid very early autumn or spring sowing dates that expose young wheat to high spore levels.

advisories.overview: Wheat stem rust / Black rust (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici) produces large, elongated reddish-brown powdery pustules on stems, leaf sheaths, and glumes, causing lodging and total crop collapse.
symptoms: Scout true stems and leaf sheaths weekly from jointing through dough stages.
Look for large, rough, diamond-shaped reddish-brown pustules that rupture the epidermis with ragged edges.
Check for black teliospore stages developing late in the season.
immediate_actions: Eradicate barberry (Berberis vulgaris) and mahonia alternate host bushes near wheat fields.
Destroy volunteer wheat and grassy weeds that provide a 'green bridge' for rust survival.
Report suspect stem rust occurrences immediately to cereal pathology authorities.
prevention: Plant stem rust resistant wheat varieties (such as those carrying Sr2-complex or Ug99-effective resistance genes).
Sow early-maturing varieties to escape late-season epidemic peaks.
Support regional cereal rust surveillance and trap-plot monitoring networks.

advisories.overview: Stripe rust / Yellow rust (Puccinia striiformis) produces bright yellow-orange powdery pustules arranged in narrow, parallel stripes along the leaf veins of adult wheat plants.
symptoms: Scout early in spring on lower leaves and south-facing slopes or sheltered field spots.
Look for distinctive long, narrow yellow stripes of powdery pustules running parallel along veins.
Check upper canopy and flag leaves closely as temperatures warm.

Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that extends vegetative vulnerability in cool weather.
Monitor weather forecasts for cool (10-15°C), moist, dewy conditions.
prevention: Plant stripe-rust resistant wheat cultivars carrying durable adult plant resistance (Yr genes).
Adopt diversified wheat variety plantings across different field blocks to slow pathogen adaptation.
Follow regional disease forecasting and early alert warnings.

symptoms: Inspect seedling emergence daily for striped and spotted cucumber beetle feeding.
Check for sudden daytime wilting of individual leaves or entire runners that fails to recover overnight.
Scout perimeter rows closest to grassy or wooded field borders.
immediate_actions: Rogue out and destroy wilted plants immediately to prevent beetle vectors from acquiring and spreading bacteria.
Deploy yellow sticky traps and monitor cucumber beetle populations closely.
Perform a field sap stringing test on cut stem ends to check for viscous bacterial strands.
prevention: Install floating row covers over young zucchini transplants until flowering begins.
Manage early-season cucumber beetle populations with IPM exclusion and trapping.
Eliminate cucurbit weed hosts around field margins.

symptoms: Inspect lower, older leaves and dense inner canopy foliage weekly.
Look for faint, round, white powdery spots on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.

Ensure plants are well-watered at the roots, as water-stressed cucurbits are more vulnerable.
Remove severely colonized senescing leaves from greenhouse facilities.
prevention: Grow zucchini varieties with high genetic resistance to powdery mildew (PMR).
Maintain adequate plant spacing in open fields and high-tunnel environments.
Avoid excessive applications of high-nitrogen fertilizer that promote dense, succulent foliage.

advisories.overview: Zucchini yellow mosaic virus (ZYMV), transmitted by aphids, causes severe leaf mosaic, blistering, shoe-string leaf distortion, stunted growth, and severely knobby deformed fruit.
symptoms: Inspect young expanding leaves for yellow mosaic mottling, bubbling, and strap-like distortion.
Examine developing zucchini fruits for extreme knobby, bumpy surface malformations.
Scout for aphid colonies on leaf undersides and growing tips.
immediate_actions: Rogue out and destroy infected plants immediately upon first symptom detection.
Do NOT compost virus-infected plants near active cucurbit plantings.
Control aphid populations using reflective silver mulches and IPM practices.
prevention: Plant ZYMV-resistant zucchini hybrids (carrying multi-virus resistance).
Apply reflective silver plastic mulch to deter winged aphid vectors from landing.
Eliminate perennial weed reservoirs (such as wild cucurbits) around field borders.
